Chapter 4. The Role of Government, Law, and Business in Sustaining Forced Labor.
Over the years, the machinery behind forced labor didn't just keep turning—it grew more tangled, more entrenched, and a lot more powerful. It wasn’t just a handful of individuals or small groups cashing in on the suffering of Black Americans. Whole institutions got involved—governments, courts, and big corporations. Their involvement made the system last, shaping not just the lives of millions, but the very future of the country.
Local and state governments were right at the heart of it. They passed laws that criminalized everyday behaviors—things like wandering without a job or even just trying to live independently. Suddenly, being poor or simply trying to get by became a crime. Police and sheriffs enforced these rules aggressively, arresting Black men and women for the smallest infractions, or sometimes making up charges altogether.
And the courts? Instead of protecting people, they became tools for oppression. Judges handed out harsh sentences, then turned prisoners over to private companies hungry for cheap labor.
The profits from this system didn’t just go into one pocket. Local officials took kickbacks for every person sent to the camps. State governments relied on money from convict leasing to build schools, roads, and other public works. Corporations struck deals with those in power, making sure they always had a steady flow of workers. The line between public service and private gain almost disappeared—replaced by a web of shared interests.
Picture this: a young man, arrested for something minor, stands before a judge who’s already decided his fate. The courtroom is just for show. The real deal's been made behind closed doors, between officials and businessmen. He’s sentenced to months, maybe years, of hard labor. His life’s traded for someone else’s profit. His family? They’re left powerless, with nowhere to turn. The very law that should protect him is now a weapon used against him.
The federal government wasn’t just standing by, either. Sometimes, it helped through inaction—and sometimes, through active support. Investigations into abuses were often half-hearted or blocked by political pressure. And when officials did try to step in, they ran into stubborn resistance from local authorities and business leaders. The result? A system that ran almost unchecked, protected by both law and custom.
Most folks outside the South had no idea just how brutal and widespread forced labor had become. Reports of abuse were brushed off as rare exceptions—not signs of a much bigger problem. The story America liked to tell about itself—that the country was moving past its racist past—remained unchallenged, even as millions continued to suffer in silence.
Over time, it became an open secret—everyone knew that government, law, and business were in on it. This alliance didn’t just shape the South’s economy; it shaped communities, families, and left deep scars that would last for generations.
And here’s the thing: the end of slavery didn’t mean the end of exploitation. The systems that came after were just as effective at controlling and profiting from Black labor. Instead of serving justice, the law was used to keep people oppressed. For so many who lived through this era, the hope of a better life always seemed just out of reach.
